title: Warm priming and surge decompression ops checklist (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working checklist and operator scratchpad for handling region-level surge decompression and warm-priming flows during regional degradations. Focus is on minimizing cold-cache amplification, avoiding cache stampedes, and keeping latency SLOs intact while shifting traffic across regions.

When to use this doc:
- Progressive degradation in a region (increased tail latency, packet loss from edge providers)
- Partial region evacuation where we want to maintain throughput using warm standby pools
- Planned evacuations (e.g., maintenance) where operator-triggered warm priming can avoid a cold-start surge

High-level goals:
- Pre-seed KV cache and prefix caches in target region before shifting significant traffic
- Compress inbound burst using staged ingress shaping so downstream model-serving queues don't back up
- Keep DNS TTLs and client backoff in sync: prefer shorter TTLs when performing aggressive shifts, but avoid too-short TTLs that cause DNS churn

Quick operator checklist (ordered):
1) Initial triage (0-5 minutes)
   - Confirm scope: which region(s) show errors/latency? look at traces and edge errors
   - Pager channels: escalate to SRE lead and serving-runtime oncall
   - Set incident flag in Slack: #sre-ops + region code (e.g., #sre-ops-eu-west1)

2) Protect control plane (5-10 minutes)
   - Pause non-essential background jobs that generate heavy KV or model warmups (ETL, nightly batch)
   - Lock automated rollouts and any canary promotion jobs

3) Warm priming the target region (10-30 minutes)
   - Identify warm-standby pool(s): dedicated GPU pools tagged warm-standby-<region>
   - Kick off KV prefix pre-seed script (see commands section) to populate hot keys and model KV caches with recent prefixes from origin region
   - Start slow ramp of synthetic priming traffic at 1% of baseline per minute, monitor queue depth and tail latency
   - If KV misses > 5% after 10 mins, increase priming to 3% and re-evaluate

4) Staged traffic shift (30-90 minutes)
   - Use weighted routing rather than abrupt cutover. Suggested weights: 5% increments every 3-5 minutes if telemetry stable
   - Ramp rules: stop ramp for any of the following triggers: model-serving error rate > 1%, P50 latency increased by >30%, queue depth > X (see metrics below)
   - If DNS TTL changes are needed, coordinate with CDN/edge owners; prefer sticky client hints where available

5) Surge decompression knobs (during and after shift)
   - Enable request coalescing at edge for identical prefixes where supported
   - Route long-tail requests to lower-cost/fallback model variant if tail latency spikes (policy: route >10s expected latency to small-model fallback)
   - Apply local rate limits per token generation to avoid single-client storms

6) Post-shift stabilization (90+ minutes)
   - Keep priming traffic at low steady-state for 1-2 H after cutover to maintain caches
   - Gradually return background jobs to normal cadence and re-enable rollouts after 3 H observation window
   - Create incident ticket/retro owner and attach priming metrics

Key runbook commands and scripts (examples)
- kvcache pre-seed (python): ./scripts/seed_kvcache.py --src-region=us-west1 --dst-region=eu-west1 --prefix=recent-hotkeys --rate=200/s --dry-run=false
- start priming job (airflow): airflow trigger_dag priming_pipeline --conf '{"dst":"eu-west1","rate_per_min":60}'
- routing weight change (kubectl or infra API): infractl routing set-weight --route=global-api --region=eu-west1 --weight=0.15
- quick rollback: infractl routing set-weight --route=global-api --region=us-west1 --weight=0.95

Important metrics to watch (dashboards):
- model_serving.errors_per_minute (should be < 1% of baseline)
- model_serving.p95_latency_ms and p99_latency_ms (watch tails closely)
- queue_depth and inflight requests per instance (trigger alarm if > 75% max)
- kvcache.hit_rate by prefix (target > 90% for seeded prefixes)
- egress_bandwidth_utilization (watch cross-region egress caps)
- dns_error_rate and dns_lookup_time (client-visible failures during TTL changes)

Operational guidance and pitfalls (notes to oncall):
- Don't reduce DNS TTL to under 30s unless you can guarantee downstream client churn won't cause more harm. Short TTLs help quick rollback but increase edge churn and can exacerbate propagation lag with some resolvers.
- Avoid mass parallel KV pre-seed from origin when origin is under stress; instead, use an intermediate read-replica or a compact snapshot export if available.
- If priming is failing because of auth/rsync issues, fall back to model artifact snapshot restore in target region rather than live replay.
- Canary vs full-weight heuristics: prefer canary if the failure mode is unknown; prefer bulk shift when origin is fully incapacitated and the warm standby is already healthy.

Open questions and follow-ups (TODOs):
- How to automate prefix selection for kvcache priming without exposing sensitive user prefixes? (privacy question)
- Can we add a rate-limiter that is token-aware rather than request-aware to better clamp multi-token storms?
- Need an experiment to validate priming rate vs hit-rate improvement across models (A/B test plan attached in linked artifacts)

Blameless post-ops checklist (after incident):
- Attach priming run logs and routing changes to the incident ticket
- Export kvcache hit-rate curves before/during/after and save as artifacts
- Run a short synthetic replay to validate that caches still have expected contents within 24 H
- If TTL was changed, log the exact TTLs and affected LB/edge provider names for the retro

Mini-retro notes from last sim (2025-01-21):
- What went well: warm priming reduced p95 spike by ~40% during initial 20m shift
- What didn't: we hit cross-region egress quota unexpectedly because synthetic priming used origin read path instead of snapshot -> add quota check before priming
- Action item: add preflight check that validates egress headroom and origin load; default to snapshot fallback if headroom < 2x estimated priming egress

Contact list (primary responders):
- SRE lead: Leila Chong (pager)
- Serving runtime: Marco Ruiz (pager)
- Networking/Edge: Aisha Patel
- Product owner fallback: Keisha Morgan

Notes to self: keep this doc intentionally lightweight. The final runbook will be split into a crisp playbook (one-pager) and a deeper appendix with scripts and telemetry links. This is the appendix-first draft and will be iterated after the next priming sim in April.
